clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic ZFYVE26 variants affecting spastizin
The Kjellin syndrome phenotype combines spastic paraparesis with a central pigmentary maculopathy causing progressive visual loss
Cognitive decline, thin corpus callosum and periventricular white-matter change are characteristic, closely mirroring SPG11
Onset is typically in childhood or adolescence with learning difficulty preceding or accompanying gait deterioration
A peripheral axonal neuropathy and distal amyotrophy are common additional features
Spastizin functions in autophagy and endosomal trafficking, and its loss impairs lysosomal recycling in neurons
Management is symptomatic and multidisciplinary, including physiotherapy, spasticity control, low-vision support and educational input
reference.pathophysiology: SPG15 is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in ZFYVE26, which encodes spastizin, a large protein that partners with spatacsin (the SPG11 protein) in autophagic lysosome reformation and endosomal trafficking. Deficiency impairs recycling of lysosomes and clearance of cellular material, leading to accumulation of storage-like material and neurodegeneration. The corticospinal tracts, cerebral white matter (with thin corpus callosum), retina and peripheral nerves are all affected, producing complicated spastic paraparesis with cognitive impairment, the distinctive Kjellin pigmentary maculopathy and an associated neuropathy. The close functional relationship with spatacsin explains the marked clinical overlap between SPG15 and SPG11.
additionalDifferentials: SPG11 (spatacsin) complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia with thin corpus callosum
SPG21 (MAST syndrome) and other complicated recessive HSPs
Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses and other storage disorders with maculopathy
Retinal dystrophies with associated neurological disease
additionalInvestigations: ZFYVE26 sequencing and deletion analysis within a complicated-HSP panel
MRI of brain demonstrating thin corpus callosum and white-matter change
Ophthalmological review with fundus imaging and electroretinography for the maculopathy
Nerve conduction studies for the associated axonal neuropathy
Metabolic and storage-disorder screen to exclude mimics
redFlags: Progressive visual loss requiring formal ophthalmological assessment
Rapid cognitive or behavioural decline prompting broader evaluation
Loss of ambulation or safe swallowing indicating advancing disease
Seizures suggesting more extensive cortical involvement
reference.prognosis: SPG15 is a progressive multisystem disorder, and many affected individuals lose independent walking and develop significant cognitive and visual impairment by adulthood, although the rate of decline varies.
pitfalls: Failing to examine the retina and missing the pigmentary maculopathy that distinguishes Kjellin syndrome
Not distinguishing SPG15 from SPG11 without complete genetic testing
Overlooking a peripheral neuropathy that contributes to disability
Attributing early learning difficulty to an unrelated cause and delaying diagnosis
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; manage spasticity with oral antispasticity agents and focal botulinum toxin, adding intrathecal baclofen where tone is refractory
Physiotherapy, stretching and ankle-foot orthoses to maintain gait, with wheelchair and seating provision as ambulation is lost
Ophthalmological surveillance and low-vision rehabilitation for the progressive Kjellin pigmentary maculopathy
Neuropsychological support, cognitive rehabilitation and carer education for progressive cognitive decline
Podiatry and orthotic management of the associated axonal neuropathy and distal amyotrophy
Treat neurogenic bladder symptoms with antimuscarinic agents and urological input
Genetic counselling with cascade ZFYVE26 testing for autosomal recessive inheritance
